Lecture 1: What is React and the Declarative Model

Interview Question

CORE

What is React, and how does its declarative, component-based model differ from plain JavaScript DOM scripting?

Imagine this scenario:

  1. Clara logs into The National Times website to read the morning investigative edition.
  2. The newsroom header displays her name in multiple places across the top navigation bar.
  3. Your plain JavaScript script runs a function to update the user name across the screen.
  4. Why does the greeting say Clara while the subscriber badge still displays Guest?
  5. Readers see conflicting user information, suspect account errors, and lose trust in the platform.
  6. The manual script updated two DOM nodes but missed the third element entirely.
  7. Today, your UI will synchronize every element automatically from a single source of truth.

Manual DOM Hunting and State Drift

In plain browser JavaScript, you build dynamic pages by manipulating the Document Object Model. Developers commonly call this the DOM. The DOM is the browser's internal tree of live C++ objects representing every HTML element on screen. To change a word on the page, your script must locate the exact element first. You call browser methods like document.getElementById or document.querySelector. Once the element is found, you overwrite its properties directly in memory. You assign new text using textContent or replace markup using innerHTML.

In a growing application like The National Times, a single piece of reader data appears across multiple sections. The subscriber's name appears in the welcome banner, the profile menu, and the subscription badge. When the user logs in, your script must find and update every single copy by hand.

Look at the naive imperative update function below:

Naive DOM Update
1function updateHeaderUser(name) {
2 const greeting = document.getElementById('header-greeting');
3 greeting.textContent = 'Welcome, ' + name;
Updates header GREETING
4 const profile = document.getElementById('nav-profile-name');
5 profile.textContent = name;
Updates navigation PROFILE
6}

When updateHeaderUser runs, it updates the greeting and the profile pill. However, notice the omission: the script forgot to query #subscriber-badge. The greeting displays Clara, but the badge still displays Guest.

This synchronization failure is called state drift. State drift happens when two interface elements that should show the same data show different values. In imperative programming, you bear two burdens: deciding what changed, and finding every affected node. As your website grows to hundreds of elements, manual hunting inevitably misses nodes.

To avoid missing individual nodes, developers often attempt to replace the entire parent container at once. They wipe the whole container using innerHTML. While this guarantees all text gets updated, it introduces a severe hidden penalty:

Destructive Replacement
1function replaceHeader(name) {
2 const root = document.getElementById('header-root');
3 const markup = `<header><h1>National Times</h1><p>${name}</p><input /></header>`;
4 root.innerHTML = markup;
WRONG: wipes container, losing input FOCUS
5}

⚡ IN THE WILD

Why does innerHTML destroy your active input focus? When you assign a new string to innerHTML, the browser parser does not compare text. It destroys every existing DOM node inside that container and creates brand-new nodes in memory. If a reader is typing in an input when innerHTML runs, that <input> element is deleted from existence. The browser recreates a new input that looks identical, but the active cursor focus is lost. Text selection vanishes, and running CSS transitions reset to their initial frames. React avoids this by comparing changes in memory and surgically updating only the text nodes that changed.

Interview Tip

To impress the interviewer: When asked why React was created, do not merely say "it makes building websites faster." Explain that React solves the fundamental problem of state drift inherent in imperative programming. In vanilla JavaScript, the developer must manually keep the DOM in sync with data across dozens of queries. React replaces this manual choreography with a declarative model. The user interface becomes a pure projection of application data: UI = f(data).

The Declarative Paradigm: UI as a Projection of Data

To permanently eliminate manual DOM hunting and state drift, modern web development relies on a paradigm called declarative UI. In a declarative system, you do not write step-by-step instructions telling the browser how to locate, create, or mutate DOM elements. Instead, you declare what the user interface should look like for a given set of data. React takes on the mechanical burden of computing the differences and physically updating the browser DOM.

The central mathematical model of React is expressed in a single governing formula: UI = f(data). This equation states that the user interface is a deterministic projection of application state. The function f takes application data as its input and returns a lightweight description of what should appear on screen. Whenever the data changes, the equation recalculates. Because the entire visual presentation is derived directly from data, two elements derived from the same source of truth can never fall out of sync.

If React recalculated the user interface by destroying and re-creating the DOM on every data change, it would suffer from the exact same focus destruction and performance penalties as innerHTML. Instead, React executes your function in JavaScript memory. It builds an in-memory tree of lightweight JavaScript descriptors, commonly called the Virtual DOM. React compares this new tree of descriptors against the previous tree. It determines the minimal set of changes required and surgically mutates only the specific DOM properties that actually changed. Living DOM nodes remain intact, preserving text inputs, active cursor focus, and CSS animations.

Key Takeaway

In React, the user interface is an ephemeral projection of data. You declare what the screen looks like for a given state, and React handles surgical DOM updates behind the scenes.

Principles of React: The Core Laws of the Declarative Model

To prepare for any technical interview, we must separate theory from application and establish the five fundamental laws governing how React replaces imperative DOM mutation with a declarative architecture. In vanilla JavaScript, the developer manually orchestrates browser DOM updates. In React, the user interface is a pure projection of application data: UI = f(data). We formalize these rules into five standalone principles.

PRINCIPLE 1

Declare UI as a Pure Function of Data Instead of Mutating DOM Nodes

You must declare what the user interface looks like for a given set of data (UI = f(data)), strictly avoiding manual DOM queries like document.getElementById or property mutations.

We should do this:
return (<h1>Welcome, {name}</h1>);
Declares UI as a pure projection of data
We should not do this:
const el = document.getElementById('title'); el.textContent = name;
Manual DOM mutation causes state drift

To understand the declarative model in an interview, you must decompose the governing formula UI = f(data) into three separate architectural tiers:

  1. The Data Input (data): Immutable snapshots of application state representing the single source of truth at a given moment in time.
  2. The Pure Projection Function (f): A deterministic function that takes data as an input and calculates the visual interface without performing outside mutations.
  3. The Virtual Descriptor (UI): A lightweight tree of plain JavaScript objects describing what DOM nodes the browser should ultimately display.

In imperative browser programming, you write sequential commands telling the browser how to locate elements, parse strings, and mutate living C++ objects. When application state changes, you must manually trace every dependent DOM node across the entire page. In declarative React, you write pure functions that return descriptions of the desired UI for any given data. React takes on the mechanical burden of computing the differences in memory and applying minimal DOM patches automatically.

Principle 1: Declarative Projection vs Imperative Mutation
1const title = document.getElementById('news-title');
WRONG: Imperative DOM hunting is fragile and manual
2title.textContent = article.headline;
3
4export default function Headline({ headline }) {
RIGHT: Declarative component projects UI directly from data
5 return (<h1 className="news-title">{headline}</h1>);
6}
PRINCIPLE 2

Drive Related Elements from a Single Source of Truth to Eliminate State Drift

You must store shared application data in a single centralized source of truth and project it outward to all dependent interface elements, eliminating synchronization failures where separate queries drift out of sync.

We should do this:
<SiteHeader reader={currentUser} />
Centralized data updates all dependent views
We should not do this:
updateGreeting(name); updateBadge(name);
Independent queries drift when updates miss

In software architecture, state drift occurs whenever multiple parts of a user interface hold duplicate representations of the same underlying data:

  1. The Imperative Synchronization Trap: In vanilla JavaScript, updating a reader name requires querying the greeting banner, the navigation bar badge, and the account drawer independently. If an exception interrupts the sequence or a query is omitted, one DOM node updates while another shows stale text.
  2. Unidirectional Projection: In declarative React, all related interface elements derive their markup from the identical data reference in the same render pass, making state drift mathematically impossible.
Principle 2: Centralized Truth vs Independent Queries
1document.getElementById('greeting').textContent = name;
WRONG: Independent queries leave elements out of sync
2
3function Header({ user }) {
RIGHT: Centralized data projects to all elements
4 return (
5 <header><h1>{user.name}</h1><p>{user.tier}</p></header>
6 );
7}
PRINCIPLE 3

Describe the Target End-State Instead of Manual DOM Transition Steps

You must declare the desired final visual state for any given condition, allowing React to compute the transition steps automatically instead of writing manual DOM mutation commands.

We should do this:
return (isLoggedIn ? (<UserMenu />) : (<LoginButton />));
Describes desired end-state for each condition
We should not do this:
el.classList.remove('hidden'); el.classList.add('active');
Manual DOM transition choreography is fragile

In technical interviews, candidates must clearly articulate the difference between choreographed transitions and state declarations:

  1. Choreographed Transitions vs Desired States: In imperative DOM programming, transitioning between signed-out and signed-in states requires finding nodes, adding classes, removing elements, and updating attributes in a precise sequence. Any missed step leaves the UI in a corrupted intermediate state.
  2. Declarative State Projections: In React, you declare two complete visual states. When the login status flips, React computes the diff and applies the exact DOM mutations needed to match the target description.
Principle 3: Desired End-State vs Imperative Steps
1function showLogin() {
WRONG: Imperative DOM transition choreography
2 document.getElementById('login-modal').classList.remove('hidden');
3 document.getElementById('user-pill').classList.add('hidden');
4}
5
6function AuthWidget({ isLoggedIn }) {
RIGHT: Declaratively describe markup for the active state
7 return (isLoggedIn ? (<UserPill />) : (<LoginButton />));
8}
PRINCIPLE 4

Treat the UI as an Ephemeral Projection Rather Than a Stateful Container

You must treat the user interface as an ephemeral visual projection of memory, never using HTML DOM elements or attributes as the primary database for storing application data.

We should do this:
const count = 5; return (<span>{count}</span>);
Stores data in JavaScript memory
We should not do this:
const count = parseInt(el.dataset.count, 10);
Reading state from DOM couples logic to markup

Interviewers frequently test whether candidates understand where state truly belongs in a modern frontend architecture:

  1. The DOM as Storage Anti-Pattern: In legacy jQuery and vanilla JavaScript, developers frequently read values from HTML data-* attributes, classes, or inner text to determine current application state. Reading from the DOM is slow and tightly couples business logic to presentation markup.
  2. Inverted Dependency: In React, application data lives purely in JavaScript memory. The DOM is treated as a dumb, disposable projection screen that React updates to reflect memory.
Principle 4: Memory Source vs DOM Storage
1function getActiveCount() {
WRONG: Storing and reading application state inside the DOM
2 return parseInt(document.getElementById('counter').dataset.count, 10);
3}
4
5function CounterView({ count }) {
RIGHT: State resides in JavaScript memory; DOM is a pure reflection
6 return (<div className="counter-display">{count} articles read</div>);
7}
PRINCIPLE 5

Rely on Virtual Reconciliation to Preserve DOM Node Identity and Active Focus

You must allow React to reconcile changes in memory and surgically patch the DOM, strictly avoiding destructive container wipes like innerHTML that destroy active input focus, text selection, and CSS transitions.

We should do this:
<header><h1>{title}</h1></header>
Surgical update preserves active input focus
We should not do this:
root.innerHTML = '<h1>' + title + '</h1>';
Container wipe destroys DOM nodes and focus

In senior engineering interviews, candidates must clearly contrast browser DOM destruction against virtual reconciliation:

  1. The Destructive C++ Cost of innerHTML: Assigning a markup string to innerHTML forces the browser engine to wipe out all existing C++ DOM nodes inside that container. Even if the new HTML structure matches the old, the physical nodes are destroyed. Active text input focus is lost, text selection collapses, and active CSS transition animations reset to their first frame.
  2. Surgical In-Memory Patching: React maintains an in-memory virtual tree of descriptors. During reconciliation, React diffs the previous descriptors against the new descriptors. It detects that only the <h1> text changed, and executes a targeted DOM mutation (node.nodeValue = title), leaving the living <input> element and active user focus completely undisturbed.
Principle 5: In-Memory Reconciliation vs DOM Destruction
1root.innerHTML = `<header><h1>${title}</h1><input /></header>`;
WRONG: innerHTML wipes container, deleting active inputs and focus
2
3function Header({ title }) {
RIGHT: React diffs in memory and patches only the h1 text node
4 return (<header><h1>{title}</h1><input /></header>);
5}

Displays subscriber membership status and reader name

To eliminate state drift, we will build a unified site header using four components assembled strictly top-down. The parent container SiteHeader.jsx holds the single data truth and distributes it downward to ReaderGreeting.jsx and SubscriberBadge.jsx. Finally, App.jsx mounts the feature at the application root boundary.

Step 1
First, we construct the parent container
<SiteHeader.jsx>

We begin by constructing the parent container SiteHeader.jsx. This component acts as the orchestrator of the site header. Inside this file, we declare our reader data once in a local constant: readerName = 'Clara Foster'. Notice that SiteHeader.jsx does not query any DOM elements. Instead, it renders JSX describing the header layout and passes readerName downward as an explicit prop to both child components:

SiteHeader.jsx
1import ReaderGreeting from './ReaderGreeting.jsx';
2import SubscriberBadge from './SubscriberBadge.jsx';
3export default function SiteHeader() {
4 const readerName = 'Clara Foster';
Declares reader data TRUTH
5 return (
6 <header className="site-header">
7 <ReaderGreeting readerName={readerName} />
8 <SubscriberBadge readerName={readerName} tier="Premium" />
9 </header>);
10}

Notice what is physically absent from SiteHeader.jsx: there are zero document.getElementById calls, zero query selectors, and zero manual string concatenations. If the value of readerName changes, both child components receive the new prop simultaneously. Because both children derive their display from the exact same variable in the parent, state drift is mathematically impossible.

Step 2
Next, we build the child component
<ReaderGreeting.jsx>

Now we build the first child component ReaderGreeting.jsx. This component has a single responsibility: display a personalized welcome greeting for the current subscriber. Inside its JSX markup, it renders a <div> element containing a <span>. It embeds the readerName variable directly inside the text using curly braces:

ReaderGreeting.jsx
1export default function ReaderGreeting({ readerName }) {
2 return (
3 <div className="header-greeting">
4 <span>Welcome back, {readerName}</span>
5 </div>
6 );
7}

Inside ReaderGreeting.jsx, the curly braces around {readerName} act as an evaluation window. When the JavaScript engine reaches {readerName}, it evaluates the variable in memory and inserts its value into the rendered text. The component does not know where readerName came from. Nor does it care if other components display the same name. It simply takes its input and returns the corresponding markup description.

Step 3
Then, we declare the child component
<SubscriberBadge.jsx>

Next, we construct the second child component SubscriberBadge.jsx. In our plain JavaScript test, this widget fell victim to state drift because the script forgot to query its ID. In React, we define SubscriberBadge to accept the shared reader data and display the membership tier alongside the name:

SubscriberBadge.jsx
1export default function SubscriberBadge({ readerName, tier }) {
2 return (
3 <div className="subscriber-badge">
4 <span className="tier-tag">{tier}</span>
5 <span className="member-name">{readerName}</span>
6 </div>
7 );
8}

What happens if SubscriberBadge manages its own reader lookup? If children query the DOM independently, timing differences cause desynchronized data. By requiring SiteHeader to supply readerName to both children, we establish a single source of truth. Both widgets are guaranteed to display the exact same user identity on every render.

Step 4
Finally, we mount the feature inside
<App.jsx>

Finally, we seal our feature by importing and mounting SiteHeader inside the top-level application component App.jsx. App.jsx acts as the root boundary of our application layout. It renders a containing <div className="newsroom-layout"> and mounts <SiteHeader /> at the top of the page:

App.jsx
1import SiteHeader from './components/SiteHeader.jsx';
2
3export default function App() {
4 return (
5 <div className="newsroom-layout">
6 <SiteHeader />
7 </div>
8 );
9}

When React renders <App />, it does not touch the physical DOM immediately. First, it executes App(), which calls SiteHeader(), which in turn calls ReaderGreeting() and SubscriberBadge(). React constructs an in-memory tree of lightweight JavaScript objects representing the entire layout. This in-memory tree is called the Virtual DOM, or in official modern documentation, the UI descriptor tree. React then calculates the physical DOM operations required and mounts the nodes efficiently into the browser window.

Component Summary

SiteHeader

The parent component orchestrates the site header layout. It declares the authenticated reader data as a single source of truth. Notice it actively distributes the name downward to both children. Why? To guarantee that all header elements remain permanently in sync.

ReaderGreetingreaderName={readerName}

This is the greeting child component. It receives the readerName directly from the parent container. Notice it owns zero state and performs zero DOM queries. When does it update? The instant its parent supplies a new name, rendering pure markup in memory.

SubscriberBadgereaderName={readerName} tier="Premium"

This is the badge child component. It receives the shared reader data and tier from the parent container. Notice it shares the exact same reader data as its sibling without any cross-component coupling, permanently eliminating state drift.

In our plain JavaScript experiment, updating a user required searching through document nodes and mutating elements by hand. When an application grows to dozens of components, that manual approach creates brittle code and state drift. React inverts this model completely. You declare components as pure functions of incoming data. React's engine then handles the DOM synchronization behind the scenes.

Where you will meet this

  1. Newsroom Headers & User Profiles: Synchronizing subscriber identity and membership level across navigation bars and sticky headers from a single parent user object.
  2. E-Commerce Shopping Carts: Rendering the active item count in a header badge, drawer preview, and checkout summary without manual DOM queries.
  3. Financial Trading Dashboards: Distributing live stock ticker prices down to transaction tickets, charts, and portfolio balance cards without risking desynchronized numbers.
  4. Multi-Step Application Wizards: Passing shared customer registration data across sequential steps and summary cards from a centralized container.

Glossary

  • Declarative UI: An architectural paradigm where code describes what the user interface should look like for a given state, leaving the runtime engine to compute and execute the necessary physical DOM mutations.
  • State Drift: A synchronization bug where multiple UI elements that should reflect the exact same data display contradictory or outdated values due to missed imperative updates.
  • Virtual DOM / UI Descriptor Tree: A lightweight in-memory tree of JavaScript objects representing the desired user interface structure, used by React to compute minimal physical DOM diffs.
  • Reconciliation: The background process by which React compares two virtual descriptor trees in memory and calculates the minimal set of host DOM mutations needed.
  • Idempotence: A mathematical property where executing a function with the same inputs produces the exact same output without side effects, forming the basis of predictable rendering.

Beyond the basics

  • The UI descriptor tree and React elements: When JSX executes, it produces plain, immutable JavaScript objects called React elements via react/jsx-runtime. React creates this UI tree from your components and uses it to compute minimal physical DOM mutations rather than traversing browser nodes directly (see react.dev/learn/understanding-your-ui-as-a-tree).
  • Purity in component rendering: A React component function must be a pure calculation with respect to its inputs; given the same data, it must always return the same JSX without mutating preexisting variables or performing outside side effects during render (see react.dev/learn/keeping-components-pure).
  • Preserving DOM identity during reconciliation: Unlike destructive replacements with innerHTML, React reconciles changes against the living browser DOM tree, updating only modified attributes and text nodes while preserving input focus, text selection, and active CSS transitions (see react.dev/learn/preserving-and-resetting-state).

Summary

Architectural Takeaways & Decision Matrix

❒ Declarative Data Flow

➔ ALWAYS declare shared application data in a single parent container and project it outward to all dependent interface elements.

➔ NEVER query or mutate the physical DOM directly with methods like document.getElementById or container.innerHTML inside React applications.

➔ IF multiple components display the same data THEN derive their output from a single source of truth to permanently prevent state drift.

❒ Reconciliation & State Storage

➔ ALWAYS treat the UI as an ephemeral projection of JavaScript memory, keeping application data strictly inside JavaScript state rather than DOM attributes.

➔ ALWAYS rely on React's in-memory reconciliation to surgically patch the DOM, preserving active input focus and living DOM node identity.

Lecture 2: Component Anatomy and the Capitalization Rule

Interview Question

CORE

What is a React component, and what rules govern how you write and name one?

Imagine this scenario:

  1. Marcus writes a new editorial card for the morning edition of The National Times.
  2. He builds a JavaScript function to display the article headline, summary, and author byline.
  3. Marcus names the function articleCard and mounts it in the layout as an articleCard tag.
  4. Why does the browser screen remain completely blank with zero errors in the console?
  5. Editors see no published story, while the terminal reports a successful build.
  6. The compiler treated the lowercase tag as an unknown native HTML element.
  7. Today, you will master component anatomy and the strict capitalization rule that powers React.

Lowercase Tags and Silent Disappearances

In standard HTML, web browsers recognize dozens of built-in tags like <article>, <header>, and <p>. These tags are defined by web standards. When a browser parses a lowercase tag name, it creates a native DOM element in memory. If the tag name is unknown, the browser still creates an empty HTML element. It does not throw an error. It simply paints nothing on the screen.

When Marcus writes a function named articleCard and places <articleCard /> in his JSX, he expects React to run his code.

Look at the naive lowercase attempt below:

Naive Lowercase Tag
1function articleCard() {
2 return (<article><h2>Breaking News</h2></article>);
3}
4
5export default function App() {
6 return (<articleCard />);
WRONG: compiles to native string, bypassing FUNCTION
7}

When App runs, the browser displays a blank space. Notice the problem: the function articleCard is never executed. The terminal reports a successful build, and the browser console stays clean.

The JSX compiler does not inspect your JavaScript scope to see if a function exists. Instead, it inspects the first letter of the tag name. If the tag begins with a lowercase letter, the compiler emits a string literal: _jsx("articlecard"). React receives this string and calls document.createElement("articlecard"). The browser creates an empty native DOM node. Your custom function articleCard() is completely ignored.

⚡ IN THE WILD

Why does a lowercase component fail silently? The JSX compiler follows a strict syntactic rule. When the tag starts with a lowercase letter, the transpiler generates _jsx("tagname"). The browser treats this as an unknown custom element. It creates an empty HTML element without styling or content. The terminal reports a successful build because the syntax is valid JavaScript. The browser console stays empty because unknown HTML tags are permitted by the HTML specification. To tell the compiler that your tag represents a JavaScript function, you must capitalize the first letter: <ArticleCard />.

Interview Tip

To impress the interviewer: When asked why React requires PascalCase for components, explain the compiler mechanism. JSX is transpiled into function calls like _jsx(). The transpiler uses the first letter to decide whether to pass a string literal ("div") or a direct function identifier (ArticleCard). Lowercase tags always become strings, bypassing your component function entirely.

Principles of React: The Core Laws of Component Anatomy and Invocation

To prepare for any technical interview, we must separate theory from application and establish the five fundamental laws governing how React identifies, instantiates, and executes component functions. In React, a component is not an HTML tag; it is a pure JavaScript function that returns user interface descriptors. We formalize these rules into five standalone principles.

PRINCIPLE 1

Always Capitalize Component Names Using PascalCase

You must name every React component using PascalCase (starting with an uppercase letter), so the compiler routes the tag to your custom JavaScript function rather than a native HTML element string.

We should do this:
<ArticleCard />
Transpiles to _jsx(ArticleCard, {})
We should not do this:
<articleCard />
Transpiles to _jsx('articlecard', {})

In senior technical interviews, explaining why React requires PascalCase requires dissecting the compiler's Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) tag name evaluation:

  1. The Lowercase Tag Pathway (Native HTML String Literal): If the tag begins with a lowercase character (/^[a-z]/), the JSX compiler assumes it represents a built-in browser host element. It emits a string literal: _jsx("articlecard", {}). At runtime, React passes this raw string to document.createElement("articlecard"). Because "articlecard" is not a standard HTML element, the browser instantiates an empty HTMLUnknownElement, ignoring your JavaScript function completely and painting a blank node.
  2. The Uppercase Tag Pathway (Component Function Identifier): If the tag begins with an uppercase character (/^[A-Z]/) or contains a dot (Article.Card), the JSX compiler treats it as an in-scope JavaScript variable. It emits the variable identifier directly: _jsx(ArticleCard, {}). At runtime, React receives a direct function reference, invokes ArticleCard(props) in memory, and mounts its rendered tree.
Principle 1: PascalCase Identifier Routing
1function articleCard() { return (<article>News</article>); }
WRONG: Lowercase tag compiles to native HTML string
2const el = <articleCard />;
Blank HTMLUnknownElement
3
4function ArticleCard() { return (<article>News</article>); }
RIGHT: Capitalized tag compiles to custom function
5const el = <ArticleCard />;
Executes component function
PRINCIPLE 2

Invoke Components Declaratively with JSX Tags Rather Than Function Parentheses

You must invoke components declaratively using JSX tags (<ArticleCard />), never calling the component function directly with parentheses (ArticleCard()).

It is best practice to do this:
<ArticleCard />
Preserves component boundary and hooks
Instead of doing this:
{ArticleCard()}
Bypasses React lifecycle and DevTools tree

To understand why calling a component with parentheses breaks your architecture in production, senior engineers analyze three runtime consequences:

  1. Fiber Node Boundary and Lifecycle: Writing <ArticleCard /> instructs React to create a dedicated Fiber node in the virtual DOM tree. React controls when to mount, reconcile, re-render, or unmount this instance independently. Calling ArticleCard() directly bypasses Fiber creation: it immediately executes the function during the parent's render phase and splices the returned JSX into the parent's children.
  2. React Hooks State Allocation: React tracks hooks by associating an internal linked list of hook records with the currently rendering Fiber node. Calling ArticleCard() directly inside a parent component binds ArticleCard's internal hooks to the parent's Fiber, risking hook order corruption and runtime crashes.
  3. DevTools Hierarchy and Profiling: React DevTools inspects the Fiber tree. A declarative tag <ArticleCard /> appears as an inspectable component node displaying its own props, state, and render timings. Calling {ArticleCard()} erases the component from DevTools entirely, flattening its elements into the parent.
Principle 2: Declarative Tag vs Function Call
1export default function App() {
WRONG: Direct function call flattens tree and breaks hooks
2 return (<main>{ArticleCard()}</main>);
3}
4
5export default function App() {
RIGHT: Declarative JSX tag creates independent boundary
6 return (<main><ArticleCard /></main>);
7}
PRINCIPLE 3

Always Return Valid JSX Markup or Null from Component Functions

You must ensure every component return statement evaluates to valid JSX markup or null, never returning undefined (which halts React rendering).

We should do this:
return (<div>Story</div>);
Valid JSX node rendered to UI
We should not do this:
return;
Implicit undefined return throws runtime error

In technical interviews, this return contract is evaluated across three distinct evaluation results:

  1. Valid React Nodes (Elements, Primitives, and Portals): A component may return a JSX element (<article />), a React Fragment (<>...</>), a string ("Breaking News"), a number (42), or an array of elements. React reconciles each of these types into corresponding DOM nodes or text nodes.
  2. The Intentional Zero-Node Render (null): Returning null is the official, intentional mechanism for conditional rendering when a component should display nothing. React keeps the component cleanly mounted in the Fiber tree, retains its hook state, and renders zero DOM nodes.
  3. The Unintentional Crash (undefined): In JavaScript, a function without an explicit return statement or with a bare return; automatically evaluates to undefined. In React, returning undefined is treated as a developer bug (such as forgetting a return statement inside a conditional guard). React throws an immediate fatal error.
Principle 3: Component Return Contract
1function EditorialBanner({ isVisible }) {
WRONG: Falling through without return produces undefined
2 if (!isVisible) return;
Undefined -> runtime crash!
3 return (<aside>Breaking Dispatch</aside>);
4}
5
6function EditorialBanner({ isVisible }) {
RIGHT: Return null to intentionally suppress rendering
7 if (!isVisible) return null;
Clean zero-node render
8 return (<aside>Breaking Dispatch</aside>);
9}
PRINCIPLE 4

Keep Component Rendering Pure with Zero Side Effects

pure calculations code that produces the same output for identical inputs without mutating outside state

You must author component functions as pure calculations, never modifying external variables or querying DOM nodes during render.

We should do this:
return (<h2>Headline</h2>);
Pure calculation produces deterministic UI
We should not do this:
window.articleCount++; return (<h2>Headline</h2>);
Side effect in render causes rendering bugs

Senior React interviews evaluate purity through three mathematical and architectural guarantees:

  1. Mathematical Projection (UI = f(data)): A pure component function is an idempotent calculation. Given identical data, it must return the exact same JSX tree every single time it executes, without depending on external mutable state or time-sensitive calculations (such as Date.now() or Math.random()).
  2. Zero Side Effects in the Render Phase: A side effect is any operation that modifies state outside the current function execution: mutating a global variable, updating the DOM manually, writing to localStorage, or firing network requests. Executing side effects during render violates React's concurrency model, where renders can be aborted, restarted, or paused by the scheduler.
  3. The StrictMode Double-Render Verification: In development mode under React.StrictMode, React intentionally executes component functions twice for every render. If a component mutates an external counter (globalCount++) during render, the counter increments by two instead of one. This deliberate double-render acts as an automated audit that immediately exposes impure functions.
Principle 4: Pure Component Execution Contract
1let globalCount = 0;
WRONG: Modifying outside variables during render
2function ArticleCounter() {
3 globalCount++;
Mutates external state during render!
4 return (<span>Count: {globalCount}</span>);
5}
6
7function ArticleCounter() {
RIGHT: Pure calculation without external mutation
8 return (<span>Articles Published</span>);
9}
PRINCIPLE 5

Declare Component Functions at Top-Level Module Scope, Never Nested Inside Other Components

You must always define component functions at the top-level scope of a module, strictly avoiding nesting component declarations inside the body of another component.

We should do this:
function Byline() { return (<span>Byline</span>); } function Card() { return (<Byline />); }
Top-level definition preserves identity across renders
We should not do this:
function Card() { function Byline() { return (<span>Byline</span>); } return (<Byline />); }
Nested declaration recreates component type on every render

In software architecture, understanding why nesting component definitions is catastrophic requires analyzing how React tracks component identity:

  1. Function Reference Identity and Remounting: When a component is declared inside another component's body, JavaScript creates a brand-new function object on every render pass of the parent. Because React compares component types by function reference (prevType === nextType), React sees a completely different component type. It destroys the previous DOM subtree, runs unmount cleanup, and remounts from scratch.
  2. State and Focus Destruction: Remounting on every render wipes all local state held by the child, causes active input focus to vanish, cancels CSS transitions, and severely degrades rendering performance. Defining components at top-level module scope guarantees a stable function reference across all renders.
Principle 5: Top-Level Definition vs Nested Component
1function ArticleCard() {
WRONG: Inner function gets fresh identity every render
2 function Byline() { return (<span>By Marcus</span>); }
3 return (<article><Byline /></article>);
Remounts every render!
4}
5
6function Byline() { return (<span>By Marcus</span>); }
RIGHT: Top-level declaration maintains stable identity
7function ArticleCard() {
8 return (<article><Byline /></article>);
Stable node identity
9}

(fragile approach)		REACT STANDARD
(robust architecture)		INTERVIEW TAKEAWAY

To master component anatomy, we will build a standalone editorial card for The National Times. We will construct the feature across four sequential steps: mounting the component in App.jsx, declaring the PascalCase function signature, writing the semantic JSX markup, and co-locating top-level helper components cleanly.

Step 1
First, we construct the application shell
<App.jsx>

We begin by constructing the parent application shell in src/App.jsx. This component provides the top-level container for our newsroom view. Notice that App.jsx imports ArticleCard and mounts it declaratively using an uppercase tag: <ArticleCard />. It does not execute the function. It hands the component reference to React:

App.jsx
1import ArticleCard from './components/ArticleCard.jsx';
2
3export default function App() {
4 return (
5 <main className="newsroom-layout">
6 <ArticleCard />
Mounts custom component via PASCALCASE
7 </main>
8 );
9}

Notice what is physically achieved here: writing <ArticleCard /> instructs React to create an independent Fiber boundary in the virtual DOM. React registers the component in its tree, schedules its render cycle, and renders its output inside the <main> container.

Step 2
Next, we declare the custom component
<ArticleCard.jsx>

Now we create src/components/ArticleCard.jsx. Notice that the function name begins with an uppercase letter: ArticleCard. This PascalCase naming guarantees that the JSX compiler emits _jsx(ArticleCard, {}) instead of a string literal. Inside the function body, we prepare the component shell:

ArticleCard.jsx
1import EditorialByline from './EditorialByline.jsx';
2
3export default function ArticleCard() {
Declares PASCALCASE component
4 return (
5 <article className="editorial-card">
6 <header className="card-header"><span className="badge">News</span></header>
7 <EditorialByline />
8 </article>
9 );
10}

Inside ArticleCard.jsx, the component returns a semantic <article> container enclosing a header badge and the <EditorialByline /> component. Because the tag begins with a capital letter, React knows to invoke the custom function rather than searching for an HTML element.

Step 3
Then, we declare the child component
<EditorialByline.jsx>

Next, we construct src/components/EditorialByline.jsx. This component renders author credentials and publication metadata. Notice that we define it at its own top-level module scope, completely separate from ArticleCard. We do not nest the declaration inside ArticleCard's body:

EditorialByline.jsx
1export default function EditorialByline() {
Top-level MODULE definition
2 return (
3 <footer className="byline-meta">
4 <span className="author">By Marcus Vance</span>
5 <span className="time">5 min read</span>
6 </footer>
7 );
8}

By defining EditorialByline at module scope, its function reference remains stable across every render of ArticleCard. React easily verifies that prevType === nextType during reconciliation, preserving the underlying DOM nodes and skipping redundant teardowns.

Step 4
Finally, we verify clean return types and execution

Finally, we verify that all components in our tree satisfy the return contract. Every component function explicitly returns valid JSX elements or null. If a component ever needs to conditionally suppress rendering, it returns null rather than falling through to undefined:

Clean Return Guard
1export function UrgentBadge({ isUrgent }) {
2 if (!isUrgent) {
3 return null;
Explicit null: clean zero-node render
4 }
5 return (<span className="urgent-badge">Urgent</span>);
6}

Notice the explicit guard clause: returning null tells React to mount zero DOM nodes while keeping the component alive in memory. It prevents the disastrous Nothing was returned from render crash that happens when functions accidentally return undefined.

Component Summary

App

The application shell mounts the editorial card inside the top-level layout. Notice it invokes the child using declarative JSX syntax <ArticleCard /> rather than a function call ArticleCard(). Why? To ensure React registers a dedicated Fiber node boundary in the virtual DOM tree.

ArticleCard

The editorial card component wraps newsroom copy in semantic markup. Notice its name starts with a capital letter ArticleCard. Why? To instruct the JSX compiler to treat the tag as a custom function reference rather than an unknown HTML tag string.

EditorialByline

The byline metadata component is declared at the top-level module scope. Notice it is never nested inside ArticleCard. Why? To maintain a stable function identity across renders, preventing costly remounting and lost state.

In standard JavaScript, functions are invoked imperatively with parentheses. React transforms this model: you write functions whose names start with a capital letter, and you invoke them declaratively as JSX elements. React manages the underlying execution, registers boundaries in memory, and keeps your interface pure and predictable.

Where you will meet this

  1. Design System Component Libraries: Writing foundational UI primitives like Button, Modal, and TextInput with strict PascalCase names and top-level module exports.
  2. Multi-Column Editorial Dashboards: Composing complex newspaper layouts by assembling independent, self-contained card and header components.
  3. E-Commerce Product Grids: Rendering repeating product cards with stable component identities, preventing full remounts during filter and sort operations.
  4. Enterprise Form Wizards: Structuring multi-step input forms using declarative component boundaries that preserve user typing focus and input state.

Glossary

  • Component: A pure JavaScript function that accepts inputs and returns a description of user interface markup as React elements.
  • PascalCase: A naming convention where the first letter of each compound word is capitalized (for example, ArticleCard), required by React to differentiate custom components from native HTML elements.
  • Fiber Node: An internal data structure created by React representing a unit of work and a component instance in the virtual DOM tree.
  • Declarative Invocation: Rendering a component by writing its tag name in JSX (<ArticleCard />), leaving React to manage instantiation and lifecycle.
  • Component Identity: The mechanism by which React determines whether two rendered elements represent the same component instance, based on function reference equality and tree position.

Beyond the basics

  • AST tag name transpilation: Modern JSX transforms compile uppercase tags into jsx(Component, props) while lowercase tags compile to jsx("tag", props). This decision is made purely at parse time by inspecting character casing (see react.dev/learn/your-first-component).
  • Why calling components as functions breaks hooks: Hooks rely on React's internal current Fiber dispatcher. Calling a component imperatively (MyComponent()) executes it within the caller's Fiber context, causing hook order mismatches when conditional branches change (see react.dev/reference/rules/rules-of-hooks).
  • Top-level declaration and remount prevention: Declaring a component inside another component re-creates the function on every render pass. Because prevType !== nextType, React completely destroys and remounts the child subtree (see react.dev/learn/preserving-and-resetting-state).

Summary

➔ NEVER declare component functions inside the body of another component; always define components at top-level module scope.

❒ Return Contract & Purity

➔ ALWAYS return valid JSX markup, a primitive, or explicit null from component functions; never return undefined.

➔ ALWAYS keep component rendering pure with zero side effects during the render phase.

3}

Lecture 3: JSX Grammar and Fragments

Interview Question

CORE

What is JSX, what syntax rules must every snippet follow, and how do Fragments group elements without wrapper nodes?

Imagine this scenario:

  1. An editor on The National Times copies formatted wire copy into a new story component.
  2. The wire copy contains an unclosed image tag, an adjacent headline, and summary text.
  3. The developer pastes the markup directly into the component return statement.
  4. Why does the local build crash instantly with fatal syntax errors across multiple lines?
  5. The development server halts, blocking the newsroom team from previewing breaking wire alerts.
  6. The compiler treated the pasted HTML as strict JavaScript rather than permissive markup.
  7. Today, you will master JSX syntax rules and use Fragments to group elements with zero DOM overhead.

Permissive Browsers vs Strict Compilers

In plain HTML, web browsers are remarkably forgiving. Browsers allow unclosed void tags like <img> or <input>. Browsers also permit multiple adjacent elements at the top level of a document. If you paste raw HTML markup into a standard .html file, the browser parses the text and paints the page.

When a developer pastes raw HTML into a React component function, the build tool halts immediately with fatal syntax errors.

Look at the naive HTML paste attempt below:

Naive Markup Paste
1return (
WRONG: Raw HTML pasted into JavaScript return statement
2 <img src="/wire-photo.jpg">
3 <h2>Breaking Dispatch</h2>
4 <p class="alert-text">Live news feed.</p>
5);

When this snippet runs through the compiler, the build tool crashes immediately. Notice the syntax errors: an unclosed <img> tag and adjacent sibling elements without an enclosing parent.

The compiler crashes because a JavaScript function cannot return multiple values. Writing return a, b evaluates both expressions but returns only the second value. Furthermore, JSX compiles into _jsx() function calls. Every _jsx() call represents a single element descriptor. You cannot pass two separate expressions to a single return statement without a wrapping structure.

Interview Tip

To impress the interviewer: When asked to explain JSX, do not call it "HTML inside JavaScript." State that JSX is a strict syntax extension that compiles into regular JavaScript function calls (_jsx()). Because functions can only return a single value, every JSX snippet requires a single root element.

Principles of React: The Core Laws of JSX Grammar

To prepare for any technical interview, we must separate theory from application and establish the nine fundamental laws governing the React compiler. In JSX, HTML markup strings do not exist. Every tag, attribute, inline style, and comment is transformed into JavaScript function calls and plain JavaScript objects. We formalize these rules into nine standalone principles.

PRINCIPLE 1

Always Return Exactly One Root Element

You must ensure every component return statement produces exactly one root element (because JavaScript functions can only return a single value).

We should do this:
return (<div><img /><h2 /></div>);
We should not do this:
return (<img /><h2 />);

A React component is a standard JavaScript function. In JavaScript, a return statement can only return a single value or expression. When you write two adjacent tags at the root level, JavaScript cannot evaluate them as a single expression. Under the hood, JSX compiles into _jsx(type, props) function calls. Just as you cannot return two separate function calls without wrapping them in an array or container object, you cannot return adjacent JSX tags.

Look at the minimal contrast below:

Principle 1: Single Root Invariant
1return (<img src="/a.jpg" alt="A" /><h2>Alert</h2>);
WRONG: Adjacent elements violate single return
2
3return (<div><img src="/a.jpg" alt="A" /><h2>Alert</h2></div>);
RIGHT: Single root container wraps children
PRINCIPLE 2

Group Siblings with React Fragments to Avoid Extra DOM Nodes

React Fragment ghost container that groups child tags in memory without creating a physical DOM node

You should group adjacent sibling elements using a React Fragment (<>...</>) rather than an extra <div> (satisfying the single-root rule without injecting wrapper nodes that break CSS Flexbox and Grid layouts).

It is best practice to do this:
return (<><img /><h2 /></>);
Instead of doing this:
return (<div><img /><h2 /></div>);

Wrapping elements in an extra <div> satisfies the JavaScript single-expression rule, but it inserts an unnecessary physical node into the browser DOM. This wrapper adds DOM memory overhead and disrupts CSS parent-child layout relationships like Flexbox and Grid. React solves this dilemma with the React Fragment shorthand (<>...</>).

The compiler transforms <>...</> into _jsx(Fragment, { children: [...] }). React evaluates the child elements in memory and mounts them directly into the host container, creating zero wrapper DOM nodes.

Principle 2: Zero-DOM Fragmentation
1return (
Compiles to _jsx(Fragment, { children: [...] })
Mounts children directly into parent with zero DOM nodes:
2 <>
3 <img src="/a.jpg" alt="Alert" />
4 <h2>Alert</h2>
5 </>
6);

⚡ IN THE WILD

Why does a wrapper div break your CSS Flexbox layout? When developers hit the single-root error, their instinctive reflex is wrapping everything in a <div>. While this satisfies the compiler, it often destroys layout styling. In CSS Flexbox and Grid, layout properties apply exclusively to direct child elements. If a parent container declares display: flex; gap: 16px;, its direct children become flex items. Placing an extra <div> wrapper around your siblings turns those elements into grandchildren. The flex container now sees only one child: the wrapper div. Your flex row layout collapses into a single vertical block, and gap spacing between items vanishes. React Fragments solve this by satisfying the compiler without creating a physical DOM wrapper.
PRINCIPLE 3

Always Close Every Tag Explicitly

You must explicitly close every JSX tag using a matching closing tag or a self-closing trailing slash (preventing unclosed void elements like <img> from halting the compiler).

We should do this:
<img src="/photo.jpg" alt="Photo" />
We should not do this:
<img src="/photo.jpg" alt="Photo">

In HTML5, browser parsers maintain hardcoded lists of void elements like <img>, <input>, <br>, and <hr> that cannot accept children, permitting closing slashes to be omitted. JSX, by contrast, enforces strict XML grammar. The compiler builds an Abstract Syntax Tree where every opening token <tag> must have an explicit matching boundary, either via a closing tag </tag> or a self-closing trailing slash <tag />. Omitting the trailing slash halts compilation instantly.

Principle 3: Explicit Tag Closing
1<input type="text">
WRONG: Unclosed void tags crash compiler
2<img src="/photo.jpg">
3
4<input type="text" />
RIGHT: Explicit self-closing slashes
5<img src="/photo.jpg" alt="Photo" />
PRINCIPLE 4

Write className and htmlFor to Match Native DOM Properties

native browser DOM property names live properties on element objects in browser memory (e.g. node.className)

You must write HTML attributes that collide with JavaScript reserved keywords using their native browser DOM property names (writing className instead of class, and htmlFor instead of for).

We should do this:
<div className="card">
We should not do this:
<div class="card">

To understand this rule in an interview, you must distinguish between three separate layers of the web platform:

  1. HTML Attributes (Markup Text): In raw HTML documents, class="card" and for="email" are static markup attributes parsed as plain text strings.
  2. JavaScript Reserved Keywords (Language Grammar): In ECMAScript, words like class (used to declare classes) and for (used to declare loops) are reserved keywords. In early JavaScript engines, using reserved words in dot-notation (element.class or element.for) triggered syntax errors.
  3. Browser DOM Properties (Living Objects): When a browser parses HTML, it instantiates living JavaScript objects in memory (such as HTMLDivElement or HTMLLabelElement). To avoid keyword collisions in JavaScript, the original 1998 W3C DOM specification explicitly mapped the class attribute to the property element.className, and the for attribute to element.htmlFor.

React does not invent className or htmlFor. When JSX compiles into _jsx("div", { className: "card" }), React updates the browser by setting the native DOM property directly (domNode.className = "card"). Because JSX operates at the level of JavaScript objects rather than raw HTML text strings, it aligns with native browser DOM properties.

PRINCIPLE 5

Write Multi-Word Attribute Names in camelCase

You must write all multi-word JSX attribute names in camelCase (such as tabIndex and readOnly to align with the browser's native DOM property interfaces).

We should do this:
<input tabIndex={0} readOnly={true} />
We should not do this:
<input tabindex="0" readonly>

This rule is not an arbitrary React design preference—it is the exact same DOM property alignment law established in Principle 4. In raw HTML documents, attribute parsing is case-insensitive, allowing developers to write <input tabindex="0" readonly autofocus> as uncapitalized text strings. However, in the browser's native JavaScript DOM API, the HTMLInputElement interface has defined these properties in camelCase since the initial W3C specifications: input.tabIndex, input.readOnly, and input.autoFocus. Because React maps JSX attributes directly to properties on native DOM nodes, it adheres strictly to the browser's established camelCase interface properties.

PRINCIPLE 6

Pass Inline Styles as JavaScript Objects, Never Text Strings

You must pass inline element styles as JavaScript objects with camelCase keys using double curly braces (writing style={{ color: 'red' }} instead of raw CSS text strings).

We should do this:
<span style={{ color: 'red' }}>
We should not do this:
<span style="color: red;">

Candidates frequently face two core interview questions regarding JSX inline styles:

  1. Why the double curly braces style={{ ... }}? There is no special "double-brace" syntax in React. The outer pair of braces {} is the JSX escape delimiter that switches the parser from markup mode into JavaScript expression mode. The inner pair { color: 'red', fontWeight: 700 } is simply a standard JavaScript object literal passed as the value.
  2. Why camelCase keys like fontWeight instead of font-weight? In the browser DOM, an element's inline styling is exposed as an instance of CSSStyleDeclaration (element.style). In JavaScript, writing element.style.font-weight is parsed as a subtraction expression (element.style.font minus the undefined variable weight), triggering a runtime syntax or reference error. The browser DOM API resolved this by mapping CSS hyphenated properties to camelCase JavaScript properties (element.style.fontWeight, element.style.marginTop). React's style prop passes this object directly to the browser's native element.style interface.
PRINCIPLE 7

Write Comments Inside Curly Braces as JavaScript Comments

You must write comments inside JSX markup as JavaScript block comments enclosed within curly braces ({/* comment */}), strictly avoiding raw HTML comment syntax (<!-- -->).

We should do this:
{/* breaking news alert */}
We should not do this:
<!-- breaking news alert -->

The JSX compiler operates as a two-state tokenizer: Markup Mode and JavaScript Mode. In Markup Mode, raw text characters are treated as literal text children, and encountering an opening angle bracket < immediately signals the parser to evaluate an element tag name. When encountering HTML comment syntax <!--, the tokenizer attempts to parse !-- as an HTML tag identifier, which is illegal syntax and halts compilation instantly. Curly braces {} serve as the explicit lexical boundary that switches the tokenizer into JavaScript Mode, where /* ... */ is safely evaluated as a standard ECMAScript block comment and erased during compilation.

PRINCIPLE 8

Preserve Hyphens for aria-* and data-* Attributes

You must strictly retain hyphens for aria-* and data-* attributes (writing aria-label and data-testid to align with W3C accessibility and DOM dataset specifications).

We should do this:
<input aria-label="Search" data-testid="search" />
We should not do this:
<input ariaLabel="Search" dataTestId="search" />

A common interview question asks why React converts standard HTML attributes to camelCase DOM properties, yet strictly preserves hyphens for aria-* and data-*. The answer lies in how React commits updates to the browser DOM:

  1. Standard Props use DOM Property Assignment: For standard attributes, React assigns values directly to object properties on the living JavaScript node (domNode.className = props.className, domNode.tabIndex = props.tabIndex).
  2. aria-* and data-* use DOM Attribute Assignment: The browser DOM does not define native JavaScript properties like node.ariaLabel. Screen readers (via the browser accessibility tree) and CSS attribute selectors ([data-testid="search-input"]) query the serialized HTML attribute string. Therefore, during DOM mutation, React calls the native browser method: domNode.setAttribute('aria-label', value) and domNode.setAttribute('data-testid', value). Because React relies on setAttribute(), it strictly preserves the official W3C hyphenated attribute names.

PRINCIPLE 9

Capitalize Custom Component Names and Keep HTML Tags Lowercase

You must start custom component names with a capitalized letter (<NewsAlert />) and built-in HTML tags with lowercase (<div>), signaling to the compiler whether to invoke a function or create a DOM element.

We should do this:
<NewsAlert />
We should not do this:
<newsAlert />

When an interviewer asks how the React compiler distinguishes between a built-in browser DOM element and a custom developer component, the answer is the Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) lexical tokenizer:

  1. Lowercase Initials (/^[a-z]/): When a tag identifier begins with a lowercase letter (such as <header> or <div>), the compiler treats it as a built-in HTML tag and emits a string literal: _jsx("header", props). At runtime, React passes that string directly to document.createElement("header").
  2. Capitalized Initials (/^[A-Z]/) or Dot-Notation (<Obj.Component>): When a tag identifier begins with a capital letter (such as <NewsAlert>) or contains property access, the compiler treats it as a scoped JavaScript variable identifier: _jsx(NewsAlert, props). At runtime, React invokes the function: NewsAlert(props).

If you write <newsAlert /> with a lowercase initial, the compiler emits _jsx("newsalert", props). The browser attempts to instantiate an unknown custom element <newsalert>, rendering nothing on the screen and never executing your component function.

JSX TAG

(core rule)

To master JSX syntax and Fragments in production, we will build a breaking news alert widget for The National Times. Having established our nine principles and reference tables in the theory, our case study introduces zero ungrounded concepts: every tag, attribute, and Fragment matches our theoretical derivation. We assemble the feature across four sequential steps.

Step 1
First, we construct the parent flex container
<App.jsx>

We begin by constructing the parent layout container in src/App.jsx. This component uses CSS Flexbox to position items side by side in a row with a defined gap. Notice that App.jsx mounts <NewsAlert /> as an immediate child of the flex container:

App.jsx
1import NewsAlert from './components/NewsAlert.jsx';
2
3export default function App() {
4 return (
5 <div className="alert-feed-flex">
6 <NewsAlert />
Mounts alert items directly in FLEX ROW
7 </div>
8 );
9}

Notice what is critical here: alert-feed-flex expects its immediate children to participate in the flex row layout. If NewsAlert renders an extra wrapper <div>, the flex items become trapped inside that wrapper, destroying the horizontal row layout.

Step 2
Next, we declare the Fragment root and void tag
<NewsAlert.jsx>

Now we create the component file src/components/NewsAlert.jsx. Applying Principle 1 and Principle 2, we declare the function and open a React Fragment <> to satisfy the single-root rule with zero DOM overhead. Applying Principle 3 and Principle 4, we place a self-closing <img /> tag with explicit className:

NewsAlert.jsx
1export default function NewsAlert() {
2 return (
3 <>
Opens lightweight FRAGMENT
4 <img className="story-photo" src="/breaking.jpg" alt="Story photo" />
Self-closing void TAG
5 <h2 className="alert-headline">Breaking Alert</h2>
Sibling headline HEADING

Notice the trailing slash on <img ... />. In HTML, void elements like <img> or <input> can omit closing tags. In JSX, Principle 3 mandates that all tags must be explicitly closed. Omitting the slash causes an immediate syntax error.

Step 3
Then, we add form controls and close the Fragment
<NewsAlert.jsx>

Next, we add form controls to allow newsroom editors to subscribe to live updates. Applying Principle 6 and Principle 7, we write a JSX comment {/* ... */} and an inline style object on the live indicator span: style={{ color: '#dc2626', fontWeight: 700 }}. We write <label htmlFor="alert-input"> to avoid the ECMAScript for loop keyword per Principle 4. Applying Principle 3, Principle 5, and Principle 8, we add a self-closing <input /> element with tabIndex={1} and aria-label. We then close the Fragment with </> and close the return statement:

NewsAlert.jsx (continued)
6 {/* Sibling form controls without wrapper */}
7 <span className="live-badge" style={{ color: '#dc2626', fontWeight: 700 }}>LIVE</span>
Inline style OBJECT
8 <label className="alert-label" htmlFor="alert-input">Subscribe:</label>
Form control LABEL
9 <input id="alert-input" className="alert-input" tabIndex={1} aria-label="Subscribe" />
Accessible input CONTROL
10 </>
Closes React FRAGMENT
11 );
12}

Notice how every single attribute mirrors the derivations from our Theory: htmlFor binds cleanly to the input's id, style takes a JavaScript object, and aria-label retains its hyphen. Because they are enclosed in <>...</>, React bundles them into a single return value without adding a wrapper <div>. All elements mount as direct children of alert-feed-flex.

Step 4
Finally, we mount the application at the root
<src/main.jsx>

Finally, we connect our application to the physical browser DOM in src/main.jsx. This file acts as the mounting bridge. It locates <div id="root"> and calls createRoot(). React then renders <App />, executing NewsAlert() and committing the elements directly into the flex container:

src/main.jsx
1import { StrictMode } from 'react';
2import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';
3import App from './App.jsx';
4
5const root = createRoot(document.getElementById('root'));
Locates host DOM
6root.render(
7 <StrictMode>
8 <App />
Mounts application tree into ROOT
9 </StrictMode>
10);

When React renders this tree, it evaluates <App />, encounters <NewsAlert />, and unpacks its Fragment. The image, headline, label, and input render directly inside the parent <div>. No wrapper node is created.

Component Summary

App

The parent component manages the top-level news alert flexbox layout. It mounts <NewsAlert /> as an immediate child of the flex container. Notice it expects its children to align in a direct horizontal row. Why? To maintain strict flex gap and item alignment across the newsroom header.

NewsAlert

The child component groups multiple sibling elements using a React Fragment. It provides the thumbnail image, headline, and subscription input. Notice it renders zero wrapper <div> nodes into the physical DOM. When does it mount? React unwraps the Fragment in memory, committing all siblings directly into the parent flex container.

In our experiment, we saw how pasting raw HTML halted the compiler. JSX is strict JavaScript syntax that requires a single root element, explicit tag closing, and camelCase attributes. By wrapping siblings in a Fragment <>...</>, we satisfied the compiler single-expression invariant while preserving our CSS Flexbox layout with zero DOM overhead.

Where you will meet this

  1. CSS Grid & Flexbox Layouts: Returning multiple grid or flex items from a child component without breaking layout alignment with extra wrapper divs.
  2. HTML Table Rows & Cells: Returning multiple <td> table data cells from a component without inserting invalid <div> tags inside a <tr>.
  3. Accessible Form Controls: Binding <label htmlFor="..."> to <input id="..." /> while applying aria-label and tabIndex without keyword collision crashes.
  4. SEO & Accessibility Trees: Keeping the browser DOM tree shallow and semantic, eliminating unnecessary <div> clutter for screen readers.

Glossary

  • JSX: A syntax extension for JavaScript that allows developers to write XML-like markup that compiles into standard _jsx() function calls.
  • React Fragment: A built-in React component (<>...</>) that groups a list of children without adding extra nodes to the physical browser DOM.
  • Single Root Invariant: The compiler requirement that every component return statement must resolve to a single JavaScript expression.
  • Self-Closing Tag: A tag that closes itself with a trailing slash (<img />, <input />), mandatory in JSX for void HTML elements that have no children.
  • DOM Property Mapping: The convention where JSX attributes match browser DOM object properties (such as className and htmlFor) to avoid collisions with JavaScript reserved words.
  • Tag Casing Rule: The compiler convention where lowercase tags denote browser DOM strings and capitalized tags denote in-scope component functions.

Beyond the basics

  • JSX compilation under the hood: The JSX transform turns <><h1>Hello</h1></> into _jsx(Fragment, { children: _jsx("h1", { children: "Hello" }) }) using the React Fragment symbol (see react.dev/learn/writing-markup-with-jsx).
  • Fragments with keys in mapped collections: While the shorthand <>...</> syntax does not accept attributes, the explicit <React.Fragment key={id}> syntax allows passing keys when rendering lists of fragments (see react.dev/learn/rendering-lists).
  • DOM property mapping: JSX attributes closely match browser DOM properties rather than HTML attribute strings; for example, class becomes className and for becomes htmlFor (see react.dev/learn/writing-markup-with-jsx).
  • Single-expression returns in JavaScript: A JavaScript return statement can only evaluate and return one value; wrapping multiple expressions in parentheses and a Fragment creates a single compound expression (see react.dev/learn/writing-markup-with-jsx).
  • Void elements and strict XML rules: In HTML5, void elements like <input>, <img>, and <br> can omit closing slashes, but JSX strictly follows XML rules where all tags must be explicitly closed (see react.dev/learn/writing-markup-with-jsx).

Summary

Architectural Takeaways & Decision Matrix

❒ Single Root & Fragments

➔ ALWAYS wrap adjacent sibling elements in a React Fragment (<>...</>) to satisfy the single-return rule without adding DOM nodes.

➔ NEVER wrap sibling elements in an unnecessary <div> when they reside inside CSS Flexbox or Grid containers.

➔ IF returning multiple siblings without a wrapper THEN use <>...</> to prevent compiler syntax errors.

❒ Tag Closing, Attributes & Syntax

➔ ALWAYS close all JSX tags explicitly, including void elements like <img />, <input />, and <br />.

➔ ALWAYS use className instead of class and htmlFor instead of for when assigning styling and form bindings.

➔ ALWAYS pass inline styles as JavaScript objects with camelCase keys (style={{ color: 'red' }}) rather than CSS text strings.

➔ ALWAYS use JavaScript expression comment blocks ({/* ... */}) inside JSX instead of HTML comment delimiters.

➔ ALWAYS keep aria-* and data-* in hyphenated kebab-case syntax.

DO THIS: wrap sibling elements in a Fragment with self-closing tags, DOM properties, and style objects
