Lecture 12: Keeping Components Pure

Interview Question

CORE

What does it mean for a component to be pure, and what breaks when it is not?

Imagine this scenario:

  1. Hellen Jones designs the editorial byline for The National Times investigative desk.
  2. The byline displays author credentials, reading time estimates, and publication timestamps.
  3. To track how many times a story is viewed, Hellen increments an external counter directly inside the byline function.
  4. In development under StrictMode, the counter suddenly jumps by two on every single page load!
  5. Why did the view counter double, and why does React execute component functions more than once?
  6. React components must be pure functions: given the same inputs, they must produce the same JSX without side effects.
  7. Today, you will master the purity contract, eliminate render mutations, and write idempotent React components.

The Purity Contract and the StrictMode Double-Render

In computer science, a pure function is a mathematical formula: given the same inputs, it always returns the exact same result, and it changes nothing outside of its own function body. React is designed entirely around this concept. Every React component you write must be a pure function. When React calls your component, the component should only calculate and return JSX describing what the screen should look like. It must never reach outside its own boundaries to mutate pre-existing variables, modify incoming props, or trigger side effects during the render pass.

When developers violate the purity contract by mutating external variables, silent bugs explode across their application.

Look at the naive attempt below, where an engineer increments a global counter inside the component body:

Naive Impure Component and External Mutation
1let guestViews = 0;
External state
2export default function StoryByline({ author }) {
3 guestViews = guestViews + 1;
Mutates outside render
4 return (
5 <div className="byline">
6 <span>By {author}</span> <small>{guestViews}</small>
7 </div>
8 );
9}

In development, React wraps your application in <StrictMode>. One of StrictMode's primary duties is to verify component purity by calling every component function twice! For a pure component, running the function twice produces the exact same JSX with zero side effects. But for our impure StoryByline, running the function twice increments guestViews from 0 to 1, and then immediately from 1 to 2. The counter doubles on every single page load! In production, concurrent rendering, server component streaming, and background pre-rendering can pause, abort, and restart rendering at any moment. If your component is not pure, these pauses and restarts corrupt application data.

⚡ IN THE WILD

Why does StrictMode render your component twice? When developers first see console.log() or counters firing twice in development, they often assume React has a bug. In reality, React's <StrictMode> intentionally calls your component functions, initializers, and reducers twice in development. Why? Because React is testing your code for purity! If a component is pure, calling it twice produces no observable side effects; the output is identical. But if a component mutates an external variable or modifies a prop array, the second run produces different results, exposing the bug immediately in development before it causes corrupted state in production.

Interview Tip

To impress the interviewer: When asked what component purity means, state that React components must be idempotent: given the same inputs (props, state, and context), they must always return the exact same JSX, producing zero mutations outside their render phase. Emphasize that StrictMode double-rendering exists specifically to detect side effects during the render phase, and explain that side effects belong exclusively in event handlers or lifecycle effects.

Principles of React: The Core Laws of Component Purity and Idempotence

To prepare for senior technical interviews, we must separate imperative scripting habits from React's functional architecture and establish the five fundamental laws governing how components maintain purity, handle derivations, and isolate side effects. In React, component execution is governed by functional idempotence and immutability. We formalize these rules into five standalone principles.

PRINCIPLE 1

Components Must Be Pure Functions with Deterministic Outputs

mathematical purity a function where the output is strictly determined by inputs with zero outside changes
deterministic execution running a component multiple times produces identical DOM descriptors every pass

You must write every component as a pure mathematical function: given the exact same props and state, it must always return identical JSX without modifying external state.

It is best practice to do this:
function Card({ title }) { return <h2>{title}</h2>; }
Instead of doing this:
let counter = 0; function Card({ title }) { counter++; return <h2>{title} ({counter})</h2>; }

In senior technical interviews, explaining why React embraces pure functions over stateful procedures highlights concurrent scheduling:

  1. Concurrent Safety: Because pure components produce no side effects during calculation, React can pause a low-priority render to process urgent user input and restart it later without leaving corrupted half-state behind.
  2. Deterministic Caching: When inputs do not change, React can safely skip rendering entirely via memoization, relying on the guarantee that output would remain unchanged.
  3. Headless Execution: Pure components can be evaluated safely in test runners, on server runtimes, or during build-time static page generation without browser DOM access.
Principle 1: Deterministic Output
1export default function StoryCard({ title }) {
RIGHT: Function output is pure calculation of props
2 return (
3 <h2>{title}</h2>
4 );
5}
PRINCIPLE 2

Never Mutate Variables Outside the Component Render Scope

external variable mutation reassigning or pushing to variables defined outside the component function
render scope isolation confining all write operations strictly to variables declared within the current execution

You must never mutate variables, objects, or arrays that existed before the render pass started, including module-level variables and global objects.

It is best practice to do this:
function Byline({ author }) { return <span>By {author}</span>; }
Instead of doing this:
let globalViews = 0; function Byline({ author }) { globalViews += 1; return <span>{globalViews}</span>; }

Interviewers evaluate whether candidates understand how external state mutations corrupt concurrent applications:

  1. Shared State Collisions: When two instances of the same component read and write to a shared module-level variable, their render orders determine the output, introducing non-deterministic race conditions.
  2. StrictMode Exposure: React's <StrictMode> catches external mutations by double-invoking render passes in development, immediately revealing duplicated counts or leaked state.
  3. State vs Scope: If data must persist across renders and trigger UI updates, it must be stored in official React state (useState) rather than raw module variables.
Principle 2: Render Scope Isolation
1export default function StoryByline({ author }) {
RIGHT: Component avoids modifying external state
2 return (
3 <span>By {author}</span>
4 );
5}
PRINCIPLE 3

Treat All Incoming Props as Strictly Read-Only and Immutable

prop immutability contract that component props must never be altered by the receiving component
mutating array methods JavaScript methods like sort and push that alter the underlying array in place

You must treat props as strictly read-only, never invoking mutating methods like .push(), .sort(), or .splice() on incoming prop arrays or objects.

It is best practice to do this:
const sorted = [...tags].sort();
Copy before sorting
Instead of doing this:
tags.sort();
Mutates parent array in place

Understanding prop immutability protects parent and sibling component data contracts:

  1. Pass-by-Reference Pitfalls: In JavaScript, objects and arrays are passed to functions by reference. Calling props.tags.push('Breaking') alters the parent component's array directly.
  2. Cross-Component Corruption: When a child mutates a prop array, any sibling component rendering that same array sees the corrupted data, triggering cascading visual bugs.
  3. Pure Derivation via Copying: Always create a shallow copy ([...tags]) or use non-mutating array methods (.filter(), .map(), .toSorted()) before modifying collections.
Principle 3: Prop Immutability and Array Copies
1export default function TagList({ tags }) {
RIGHT: Creates shallow copy before sorting array
2 const sortedTags = [...tags].sort();
3 return (
4 <div>{sortedTags.join(', ')}</div>
5 );
6}
PRINCIPLE 4

Local Mutation Created During the Current Render Is Fully Permitted

local mutation modifying newly instantiated objects that have no external references
temporary rendering scratchpad using local variables to assemble markup or calculate derived data cleanly

You are completely permitted to mutate variables, arrays, and objects that you created locally within the component function during the current render pass.

It is best practice to do this:
const localList = []; for (let i = 0; i < count; i++) { localList.push(<span key={i} />); } return <div>{localList}</div>;
Instead of doing this:
sharedList.push(<span />); return <div>{sharedList}</div>;
Mutating shared external array

Purity does not mean forbidding all mutations; it forbids mutating things that existed before render:

  1. Isolated Lifecycles: Variables created inside a component function exist only in that function's call stack. No outside component or prior render pass has access to them.
  2. Scratchpad Flexibility: You can freely declare an empty array, run an imperative loop to populate it, sort it, and return it inside JSX without violating React's purity contract.
  3. Zero Observable Side Effects: Because the newly created object is confined to the local stack frame, mutating it produces zero observable changes in external systems.
Principle 4: Safe Local Mutation
1export default function CupList({ count }) {
RIGHT: Modifying local variables within render is safe
2 const cups = [];
3 for (let i = 1; i <= count; i++) {
4 cups.push(<span key={i}>Cup #{i}</span>);
5 }
6 return (<div>{cups}</div>);
7}
PRINCIPLE 5

Confine Side Effects to Event Handlers and Lifecycle Effects

side effect quarantine isolating external mutations to dedicated response phases outside render
event handler response user-triggered actions that execute after rendering completes

You must quarantine all side effects (such as network requests, DOM mutations, timers, and storage writes) inside event handlers or lifecycle effects, never in the render body.

It is best practice to do this:
function handleClick() { updateDatabase(item.id); } return ( <button onClick={handleClick} /> );
Instead of doing this:
updateDatabase(item.id); return <button />;
Runs during render

Senior developers cleanly separate render-time calculations from side-effect executions:

  1. Render vs Commit Phases: React's render phase calculates virtual DOM descriptors and must remain pure. The commit phase updates the DOM, after which effects and event handlers run.
  2. User-Triggered Mutations: Operations that change data (submitting a form, navigating, saving to local storage) belong in event handlers like onClick or onSubmit where execution is intentional.
  3. Automated Lifecycle Synchronization: Side effects that must synchronize with DOM mounting or external subscriptions belong in dedicated lifecycle hooks (useEffect), never raw component bodies.
Principle 5: Quarantining Side Effects
1export default function LikeButton({ storyId }) {
RIGHT: Side effects belong in event handlers
2 function handleLike() {
3 sendLikeRequest(storyId);
4 }
5 return (
6 <button onClick={handleLike}>Like</button>
7 );
8}

To master component purity and understand how to perform safe local derivations, we will construct the editorial byline for The National Times. We will progress across four sequential steps: constructing the article view in src/components/ArticleView.jsx, building the pure byline in src/components/StoryByline.jsx, declaring the tag list in src/components/TagList.jsx, and mounting the application inside src/App.jsx.

Component Summary

The feature container provides article data to the tree. It owns the CURRENT_ARTICLE object and passes immutable props downward. Notice it performs zero mutations on incoming objects. Why? To maintain a clean, read-only data contract with the rest of the application.

StoryBylineauthor={...} wordCount={...} tags={...}

The pure coordinator component derives metadata from props. It calculates estimated reading time locally from wordCount. Notice it touches zero external variables outside its body. This guarantees that rendering twice in StrictMode produces identical output without state drift.

The terminal tag control demonstrates safe local mutation. It creates a local copy of tags using the spread operator before sorting. When does React allow mutations? Only on newly created objects within the same render pass, ensuring the parent's array remains 100% untouched.

In our experiment, we replaced external variable mutations and in-place prop modifications with pure mathematical derivations and safe local array copies. By respecting the purity contract, we guaranteed that our components remain completely idempotent, eliminating StrictMode glitches and ensuring flawless concurrent rendering.

Where you will meet this

  1. Server-Side Rendering & Streaming: Ensuring that rendering components on a Node.js server produces zero cross-request memory leaks or shared state contamination.
  2. Concurrent Suspense Boundaries: Allowing React to pause rendering during slow network requests and restart without leaving half-mutated data behind.
  3. Data Sorting & Filtering: Displaying table data in sorted or filtered orders by creating shallow copies ([...items].sort()) instead of mutating raw state arrays.
  4. Optimistic UI Updates: Rendering predictive UI changes safely, knowing that if an action fails, rolling back requires no cleanup of corrupted render-time mutations.

Glossary

  • Pure Component: A component that behaves as a mathematical function: given the same inputs, it always returns the same JSX without side effects.
  • Idempotence: The property of an operation where executing it multiple times produces the exact same result as executing it once.
  • Side Effect: Any observable change outside the current function execution, such as mutating global variables, timers, or DOM mutations.
  • Render Phase: The phase where React executes component functions to calculate the new JSX descriptor tree; must be 100% pure.
  • Local Mutation: Mutating objects, arrays, or variables that were freshly created inside the component body during the current render pass.

Beyond the basics

  • Keeping components pure: The official React documentation details the purity contract, why purity matters, and how to avoid bugs (see react.dev/learn/keeping-components-pure).
  • Detecting impure calculations with StrictMode: How React uses StrictMode double-rendering in development to find impure side effects (see react.dev/learn/keeping-components-pure#detecting-impure-calculations-with-strictmode).
  • Local mutation in React: Why mutating variables created inside the same render pass is completely allowed and safe (see react.dev/learn/keeping-components-pure#local-mutation-your-components-little-secret).
  • Where you can cause side effects: Why side effects belong in event handlers and effects rather than the render pass (see react.dev/learn/keeping-components-pure#where-you-_can_-cause-side-effects).
  • Why React cares about purity: How pure components enable concurrent rendering, memoization, and server streaming (see react.dev/learn/keeping-components-pure#why-does-react-care-about-purity).

Lecture 13: Responding to Events and Callback Props

Interview Question

CORE

How do you respond to user events like clicks and typing, and how do callback props communicate back to parents?

  • James Cooper designs the live wire feed for The National Times investigative desk.
  • The wire feed features interactive article cards with nested bookmark and share controls.
  • To handle clicks, James writes onClick={saveArticle()} directly inside the bookmark button.
  • The function executes immediately on page load, and clicking a bookmark opens the entire article!
  • Why did the action fire during rendering, and why did the nested click trigger the parent card?
  • React event handlers must be passed as function references, and nested clicks require propagation control.
  • Today, you will master event handler syntax, halt unwanted bubbling, and pass callback props cleanly.

The Invocation Trap and Event Bubbling

In React, responding to user interaction requires understanding the difference between passing a function and calling it. When you attach an event handler to a JSX element, React expects a function reference. If you append parentheses to the function name, JavaScript executes that function immediately during the render pass, long before any user touches the keyboard or mouse. Understanding this distinction is essential for writing responsive, bug-free components.

When developers write onClick={handleClick()}, the function runs as React evaluates the JSX. Its return value (usually undefined) is then assigned to the onClick prop, leaving the button inert when the user actually clicks it. Worse, if handleClick() triggers a state change or an external action, executing it during render can cause an immediate crash or an infinite re-render loop. Look at the naive implementation:

Naive Event Handler and Unchecked Bubbling
1export default function StoryCard({ story, onSelect }) {
2 function handleBookmark() { console.log('Saved:', story.id); }
3 return (
4 <article onClick={() => onSelect(story.id)}>
5 <h3>{story.title}</h3>
6 <button onClick={handleBookmark()}>Bookmark</button>
7 </article>
8 );
9}

Notice line 6: onClick={handleBookmark()}. The parentheses cause handleBookmark to execute immediately when StoryCard renders. Furthermore, even if we pass the function reference properly as onClick={handleBookmark}, clicking the button will bubble up through the DOM tree, firing the outer <article>'s onClick handler as well! A user attempting to save a story accidentally triggers navigation to that story.

⚡ IN THE WILD

Why does React wrap browser events in SyntheticEvent? In the browser DOM, event implementations historically varied across browser engines. React normalizes all native events into a unified SyntheticEvent wrapper that matches the W3C event specification. Under the hood in React 19, React attaches event listeners at the root DOM container rather than individual DOM nodes. This event delegation architecture provides identical cross-browser behavior, improves memory efficiency, and ensures methods like e.stopPropagation() and e.preventDefault() work consistently across every platform.

Interview Tip

To impress the interviewer: When asked how React handles events, emphasize that React passes function references, not function invocations. Explain that React uses event delegation at the root container to manage synthetic events efficiently. Clarify that callback props enable unidirectional data flow: parents pass functions downward, and children invoke them upward with parameters. Finally, highlight that stopping propagation (e.stopPropagation()) is critical in nested interactive components to isolate user gestures.

Principles of React: The Core Laws of Event Handling and Callback Communication

To prepare for senior technical interviews, we must separate naive scripting habits from React's event architecture and establish the five fundamental laws governing how components handle user gestures, prevent bubbling, and communicate across component boundaries. In React, event handling is governed by declarative function binding, propagation control, and unidirectional callback contracts. We formalize these rules into five standalone principles.

PRINCIPLE 1

Pass Event Handlers as Function References, Never Call Them in JSX

function reference passing an uninvoked identifier like handleClick to wait for interaction
immediate invocation appending parentheses like handleClick() executing at render time

You must pass event handlers as direct function references rather than calling them with parentheses, ensuring they execute only when the user triggers the event.

It is best practice to do this:
<button onClick={handleClick}> Save Article </button>
Instead of doing this:
<button onClick={handleClick()}> Save Article </button>

In senior technical interviews, explaining why event handlers must be passed as references rather than invoked in JSX highlights render lifecycle fundamentals:

  1. Render-Time Execution: Appending parentheses (onClick={handleClick()}) executes the function immediately during the render pass, long before any user interacts with the element.
  2. Return Value Trap: When a handler runs during render, React receives its return value (typically undefined) as the handler, leaving the button inert when clicked.
  3. Infinite Loop Prevention: If the handler updates state or makes network requests, invoking it during render triggers an immediate re-render, creating an instant infinite execution loop.
Principle 1: Passing Handler References
1export default function SaveButton({ onSave }) {
RIGHT: Passes function reference without calling it
2 return (
3 <button onClick={onSave}>Save</button>
4 );
5}
PRINCIPLE 2

Wrap Handlers in Inline Functions When Passing Arguments

inline arrow handler an anonymous function wrapper that defers invocation until clicked
parameter forwarding delivering dynamic identifiers or record payloads to handler callbacks

You must wrap event handlers in an inline arrow function whenever passing custom arguments, preventing immediate execution while delivering necessary parameters.

It is best practice to do this:
<button onClick={() => handleSelect(id)}> Read </button>
Instead of doing this:
<button onClick={handleSelect(id)}> Read </button>

Interviewers test whether candidates understand parameter forwarding without accidentally triggering render-time execution:

  1. Evaluation vs Deferral: Writing handleSelect(id) executes immediately during JSX evaluation. Wrapping it in () => handleSelect(id) creates a function reference that waits for the user event.
  2. Closure Scope Capture: The inline arrow function captures current props and state in its closure, ensuring the handler always receives fresh parameter values upon execution.
  3. Compiler Optimization: Modern JavaScript engines and React 19 handle short inline arrow functions efficiently, making them the standard idiom for parameterised event callbacks.
Principle 2: Parameterised Arrow Handlers
1export default function StoryLink({ id, onSelect }) {
RIGHT: Wraps handler in arrow function to pass ID
2 return (
3 <button onClick={() => onSelect(id)}>Open</button>
4 );
5}
PRINCIPLE 3

Stop Event Propagation to Prevent Parent Trigger Collisions

event bubbling native DOM traversal where events bubble up from child to ancestors
propagation isolation stopping event traversal at the child boundary using stopPropagation

You must call e.stopPropagation() on nested interactive elements to prevent events from bubbling up the DOM tree and firing unwanted parent handlers.

It is best practice to do this:
function handleBookmark(e) { e.stopPropagation(); onBookmark(storyId); }
Instead of doing this:
function handleBookmark() { // Bubbles to parent card! onBookmark(storyId); }

Explaining event bubbling in senior technical interviews reveals your command of both the DOM specification and React's synthetic event system:

  1. Bubbling Traversal: In both native DOM and React, click events bubble up from the target element through all parent containers until reaching the document root.
  2. Parent Collision Prevention: In nested layouts (such as a bookmark button inside a clickable card), failing to call e.stopPropagation() fires both actions simultaneously.
  3. Synthetic Event Safety: React wraps native events in a SyntheticEvent wrapper, ensuring e.stopPropagation() operates consistently across all target browsers.
Principle 3: Stopping Event Propagation
1export default function Bookmark({ id, onSave }) {
RIGHT: Stops bubbling before executing bookmark
2 function handleClick(e) {
3 e.stopPropagation();
4 onSave(id);
5 }
6 return <button onClick={handleClick}>Save</button>;
7}
PRINCIPLE 4

Prevent Default Browser Actions Declaratively in Handlers

default browser action native browser reactions like page reload on form submit
synthetic event interception preventing native browser actions using preventDefault

You must explicitly call e.preventDefault() inside event handlers to stop default browser behaviors like form reloads or link navigation.

It is best practice to do this:
function handleSubmit(e) { e.preventDefault(); onSearch(query); }
Instead of doing this:
function handleSubmit() { // Page reloads and wipes state! onSearch(query); }

Handling native browser defaults demonstrates why Single Page Applications rely on event interception:

  1. Form Reload Prevention: HTML <form> submissions trigger a full browser page refresh by default; calling e.preventDefault() retains application state in memory.
  2. Controlled Navigation: Intercepting link clicks allows client-side routers to render new views instantly without requesting a fresh HTML document from the server.
  3. Explicit Interception: Unlike some frameworks where returning false cancels events, React strictly requires calling the standard e.preventDefault() method.
Principle 4: Preventing Default Actions
1export default function SearchForm({ onSearch }) {
RIGHT: Calls preventDefault to stop full-page reload
2 function handleSubmit(e) {
3 e.preventDefault();
4 onSearch();
5 }
6 return <form onSubmit={handleSubmit} />;
7}
PRINCIPLE 5

Use Callback Props for Inverse Data Flow from Child to Parent

unidirectional data flow React law where data flows down via props and events bubble up
inverse callback prop passing a function downward so a child can emit data upward

You must pass callback functions downward as props to allow child components to notify parent containers of user interactions without mutating parent state.

It is best practice to do this:
<StoryCard onSelect={handleSelect} /> onClick={() => onSelect(story.id)}
Parent passes callback down
Child invokes callback on click
Instead of doing this:
story.isSelected = true;
Child mutates parent directly

Unidirectional data flow is React's cornerstone architectural pattern, and callback props are its voice:

  1. Single Source of Truth: Parents own the state or business logic; children remain pure presentation layers that report user gestures without owning persistent data.
  2. Encapsulated Notification: Passing callback props (conventionally named on[Event], like onSelect) decouples the child's UI from the parent's business implementation.
  3. Parameterised Upward Flow: Children can pass arguments back upward through the callback (e.g. onSelect(story.id)), informing the parent exactly what entity was touched.
Principle 5: Inverse Callback Props
1export default function StoryCard({ story, onSelect }) {
RIGHT: Child invokes callback prop to inform parent
2 return (
3 <article onClick={() => onSelect(story.id)}>
4 <h3>{story.title}</h3>
5 </article>
6 );
7}

To master event handling and witness how callback props enable clean inverse data flow, we will construct the live wire feed for The National Times. We will progress across four sequential steps: constructing the parent feed in src/components/WireFeed.jsx, building the interactive story card in src/components/StoryCard.jsx, declaring the nested bookmark button in src/components/BookmarkButton.jsx, and mounting the application inside src/App.jsx.

Step 1
First, we construct the parent feed container
<WireFeed.jsx>

We begin by constructing src/components/WireFeed.jsx. This component acts as the orchestrating container. It accepts a stories array and two callback props: onSelect and onBookmark. It iterates over the stories, rendering a StoryCard for each record and forwarding the callback handlers:

src/components/WireFeed.jsx
1import StoryCard from './StoryCard.jsx';
2export default function WireFeed({ stories, onSelect, onBookmark }) {
3 return <section className="feed-container">
4 <h2>Live Wire Desk</h2>
5 {stories.map((story) => (
6 <StoryCard key={story.id} story={story}
7 onSelect={onSelect} onBookmark={onBookmark} />
8 ))}
9 </section>;
10}

Notice lines 7 and 8: WireFeed forwards onSelect and onBookmark downward as props. The parent container owns the business logic for selecting and bookmarking articles, but delegates the interactive presentation to child components.

Step 2
Next, we build the interactive story card
<StoryCard.jsx>

Now we create src/components/StoryCard.jsx. This component displays the story category, title, and mounts the nested BookmarkButton. Clicking the outer card triggers the onSelect callback with the story's ID:

src/components/StoryCard.jsx
1import BookmarkButton from './BookmarkButton.jsx';
2export default function StoryCard({ story, onSelect, onBookmark }) {
3 return (
4 <article className="story-card" onClick={() => onSelect(story.id)}>
5 <span className="story-category">{story.category}</span>
6 <h3 className="story-headline">{story.title}</h3>
7 <BookmarkButton storyId={story.id} onBookmark={onBookmark} />
8 </article>
9 );
10}

Notice line 4: onClick={() => onSelect(story.id)}. We wrap onSelect(story.id) inside an inline arrow function. This ensures onSelect is not called during render, but instead executes only when the user clicks the card, passing story.id upward to the parent container.

Step 3
Then, we declare the nested bookmark button
<BookmarkButton.jsx>

Next, we build src/components/BookmarkButton.jsx. Because this button sits directly inside the clickable <article> card, clicking it would naturally bubble up and trigger StoryCard's onClick. To prevent this collision, we intercept the event and call e.stopPropagation():

src/components/BookmarkButton.jsx
1export default function BookmarkButton({ storyId, onBookmark }) {
2 function handleClick(e) {
3 e.stopPropagation();
4 onBookmark(storyId);
5 }
6 return <button className="bookmark-btn" onClick={handleClick}>
7 Bookmark
8 </button>;
9}

Notice lines 3 and 4: e.stopPropagation() prevents the click from bubbling to the parent StoryCard, ensuring only onBookmark runs. This cleanly isolates nested user gestures while maintaining inverse data flow!

Step 4
Finally, we mount the application inside App
<App.jsx>

Finally, we complete our scenario in src/App.jsx. We define a mock stories array and implement the concrete callback handlers handleSelect and handleBookmark:

src/App.jsx
1import WireFeed from './components/WireFeed.jsx';
2const STORIES = [
3 { id: 's1', title: 'Tech Stocks Rebound', category: 'Markets' },
4 { id: 's2', title: 'Clean Energy Accord Signed', category: 'World' },
5];
6export default function App() {
7 function handleSelect(id) { console.log('Selected:', id); }
8 function handleBookmark(id) { console.log('Bookmarked:', id); }
9 return <WireFeed stories={STORIES} onSelect={handleSelect} onBookmark={handleBookmark} />;
10}

Because our event handling is declarative and propagation is controlled, clicking an article card selects it cleanly, while clicking the bookmark button saves the article without triggering card selection.

Component Summary

WireFeedstories={...} onSelect={...} onBookmark={...}

The feed container orchestrates the live stream. It accepts story collections and event handlers, forwarding them to individual cards. Notice how it decouples parent state management from child layout concerns.

StoryCardstory={...} onSelect={...} onBookmark={...}

The interactive card handles article selection. It wraps its callback in an inline arrow function () => onSelect(story.id) to deliver parameters upon user click without firing during render.

BookmarkButtonstoryId={...} onBookmark={...}

The nested interactive button protects parent boundaries. It calls e.stopPropagation() before invoking onBookmark(storyId), preventing accidental card navigation while reporting clicks upward.

In our experiment, we replaced premature render invocations and unstopped bubbling with declarative function references, parameterised arrow handlers, and propagation isolation. By passing callback props downward, we preserved unidirectional data flow while enabling children to communicate user interactions back to parents cleanly.

Where you will meet this

  1. Modal and Dropdown Overlays: Stopping propagation on inner modal containers so clicking inside the dialog does not bubble up to the backdrop and close it.
  2. Interactive Data Tables: Wrapping table rows with row-selection clicks while providing independent edit or delete action buttons in child cells.
  3. Form Submissions: Intercepting form submission events with e.preventDefault() to validate inputs and transmit data via asynchronous fetch requests without full-page reloads.
  4. Custom Compound Components: Passing callback props through tabs, accordions, and menu items to notify the root coordinator when selections change.

Glossary

  • SyntheticEvent: A cross-browser wrapper around the browser's native event object, normalizing behavior and supporting event delegation.
  • Event Delegation: Attaching a single event listener at the root container to handle events from all descendant nodes efficiently.
  • Event Bubbling: The native process where an event triggered on a child node traverses upward through ancestor DOM nodes until handled or stopped.
  • Propagation: The traversal path of an event through the DOM tree, which can be halted using e.stopPropagation().
  • Callback Prop: A function passed from parent to child as a prop, invoked by the child to communicate events upward.

Beyond the basics

  • Responding to events: The official React documentation on handling events, passing arguments, and avoiding common traps (see react.dev/learn/responding-to-events).
  • Event propagation and bubbling: How event bubbling works in React and how to stop propagation cleanly (see react.dev/learn/responding-to-events#event-propagation).
  • Preventing default behavior: How to prevent native browser form submissions and navigation using preventDefault (see react.dev/learn/responding-to-events#preventing-default-behavior).
  • Naming event handler props: Standard conventions for naming event handlers and callback props in component libraries (see react.dev/learn/responding-to-events#naming-event-handler-props).
  • Event delegation in React 19: How React attaches root-level listeners to optimize performance and memory footprint (see react.dev/reference/react-dom/components/common#react-event-object).

Summary

Architectural Takeaways & Decision Matrix

❒ Event Handler Binding

➔ ALWAYS pass event handlers as function references: onClick={handleClick}.

➔ NEVER call event handlers with parentheses in JSX: onClick={handleClick()}.

➔ ALWAYS wrap handlers in an inline arrow function when passing arguments: onClick={() => handleSelect(id)}.

❒ Propagation & Defaults

➔ ALWAYS call e.stopPropagation() when nesting interactive controls inside clickable containers.

➔ ALWAYS call e.preventDefault() inside form submit handlers to prevent full-page browser reloads.

➔ ALWAYS pass callback props downward (on[Event]) to preserve unidirectional data flow when children notify parents.

DO THIS: pass a function reference or arrow function to wait for user interaction

code.txt
1export default function ActionButton({ onSave }) {
2 return <button onClick={onSave}>Save</button>;
3}

DO NOT DO THIS: call the handler with parentheses in JSX, executing it at render time

code.txt
1export default function ActionButton({ onSave }) {
2 return <button onClick={onSave()}>Save</button>;
3}
